description: A prototype dependency chain modelled on a first-year undergraduate economics foundations module, in the same node/edge shape a chain-generation LLM call against dependency_chains would produce.

nodes.name: Scarcity & Opportunity Cost
nodes.description: The basic economic problem: unlimited wants versus limited resources, and the true cost of any choice as the next best alternative given up.

nodes.name: Production Possibility Frontier
nodes.description: A curve showing the maximum feasible combinations of two goods an economy can produce given fixed resources and technology, illustrating opportunity cost and trade-offs.

nodes.name: Specialisation & Comparative Advantage
nodes.description: Why individuals, firms and countries gain by specialising in producing what they have a comparative advantage in and trading for the rest.

nodes.name: Law of Demand
nodes.description: The inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded, and what the demand curve represents.

nodes.name: Determinants of Demand
nodes.description: Non-price factors — income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations — that shift the entire demand curve rather than moving along it.

nodes.name: Law of Supply
nodes.description: The relationship between price and quantity supplied, and what the supply curve represents.

nodes.name: Determinants of Supply
nodes.description: Non-price factors — input costs, technology, number of sellers — that shift the entire supply curve.

nodes.name: Market Equilibrium
nodes.description: Where demand and supply curves intersect, setting the market-clearing price and quantity, and how the price mechanism restores equilibrium after a shock.

nodes.name: Price Elasticity of Demand
nodes.description: How responsive quantity demanded is to a change in price, and what determines whether demand is elastic or inelastic.

nodes.name: Price Elasticity of Supply
nodes.description: How responsive quantity supplied is to a change in price.

nodes.name: Income Elasticity of Demand
nodes.description: How responsive demand is to a change in income — used to classify goods as normal, inferior, or luxury.

nodes.name: Cross Elasticity of Demand
nodes.description: How responsive demand for one good is to a price change in another — used to classify goods as substitutes or complements.

nodes.name: Marginal Utility
nodes.description: The extra satisfaction from consuming one more unit of a good, and why it tends to diminish as consumption increases.

nodes.name: Indifference Curves & MRS
nodes.description: Curves representing combinations of two goods that give a consumer equal satisfaction, and the marginal rate of substitution between them.

nodes.name: Budget Constraint
nodes.description: The combinations of two goods a consumer can afford given their income and the goods' prices.

nodes.name: Consumer Optimisation
nodes.description: How a rational consumer chooses the affordable bundle that maximises utility, where the indifference curve is tangent to the budget constraint.

nodes.name: Deriving the Demand Curve
nodes.description: Deriving the individual demand curve by tracing how the utility-maximising choice changes as price varies.

nodes.name: Consumer Surplus
nodes.description: The difference between what consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay, shown as the area under the demand curve and above price.

nodes.name: Costs of Production
nodes.description: Fixed costs, variable costs, and how marginal and average costs behave as output changes in the short run.

nodes.name: Profit Maximisation
nodes.description: The profit-maximising output rule: produce where marginal cost equals marginal revenue.

nodes.name: Deriving the Supply Curve
nodes.description: Deriving the firm's supply curve from its marginal cost curve above the shutdown point.

nodes.name: Producer Surplus
nodes.description: The difference between the price producers receive and the minimum they'd be willing to accept, shown as the area above the supply curve and below price.

nodes.name: Allocative Efficiency & Total Welfare
nodes.description: How competitive equilibrium maximises total welfare (consumer plus producer surplus), and what allocative efficiency means.

nodes.name: Price Ceilings & Floors
nodes.description: The effects of price ceilings and price floors on quantity, shortages, surpluses, and welfare, given the relevant elasticities.

nodes.name: Taxes, Subsidies & Incidence
nodes.description: How a tax or subsidy shifts the effective supply or demand curve, and how its burden splits between buyers and sellers depending on elasticity.

nodes.name: Externalities
nodes.description: Costs or benefits of a transaction that fall on third parties, and why this causes markets to over- or under-produce relative to the social optimum.

nodes.name: Public Goods & Free-Rider Problem
nodes.description: Goods that are non-excludable and non-rival, why free markets under-provide them, and the free-rider problem.

nodes.name: Circular Flow of Income
nodes.description: The flow of income, spending, and output between households and firms, and how it extends to include government, financial and overseas sectors.

nodes.name: Measuring GDP
nodes.description: Measuring the total value of output in an economy via the output, income, and expenditure approaches, and why they should be equal.

nodes.name: Inflation
nodes.description: A sustained rise in the general price level, how it's measured, and its main causes.

nodes.name: Unemployment
nodes.description: How unemployment is measured and classified (frictional, structural, cyclical), and its economic costs.

nodes.name: The Business Cycle
nodes.description: The recurring pattern of expansion and contraction in GDP, employment, and inflation around the long-run trend.
